Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it — a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# entire-api — agent notes

Per-jurisdiction Go service: HTTP API + two NATS workers (repo-activity,
user-activity) over two Postgres stores (`repo`, `usr` schemas). See
[README.md](./README.md) for architecture and [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md)
for build/test.

## Conventions an agent must not get wrong

- **Database migrations use a UTC-timestamp version, never a hand-picked
  integer.** Create them with `scripts/new-migration.sh <repo|user> <name>` →
  `internal/store/migrations/<store>/YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_<name>.sql`. goose tracks by
  the filename's version number and silently skips any version `≤` the current
  DB version, so two PRs picking the same next integer (e.g. both `016_…`) make
  one migration vanish with no error. Leave the existing `001…0NN` files as-is.
  Full rationale: [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md#database-migrations).
- **Never renumber or edit an already-merged migration** — add a new
  (timestamped) one. They're applied in every environment.
- **A `trailforge.NewServiceForge` reason must be registered in entiredb's Core
  before it works, and registering it takes two edits there.** The reason string
  is a cross-repo contract with no enforcement on either side: Core admits an
  exact `(workload, reason)` pair, and nothing here fails when it doesn't. In
  `entiredb`'s `core/api/sts_token.go` you need **both** a row in
  `githubInstallationTokenCapabilities` *and* the reason added to that
  authority's arm of `validFor` — a row without the `validFor` entry is still
  rejected. Grep entiredb for the reason string in the same change that
  introduces it here.

  This fails silently by design: every service-forge caller is best-effort, so a
  denied mint is logged and swallowed and the feature simply never acts. Two
  shipped dead this way (`runner_checks_failed`, `trail_gate_checks_resync`). One
  was worse than a no-op — `gaterecompute` treats a failed check-run read as
  fail-closed, so the denied mint flipped the checks gate to a **blocking
  `error`**, meaning the resync route broke the gate it exists to repair. If a
  forge-backed feature does nothing in prod and nothing is in the logs, check
  the reason is admitted before reading any further.
- **Run `mise run build`, `mise run vet`, `mise run lint` before pushing.**
  Integration tests (`mise run test:integration`) need Docker and self-skip
  without `ACTIVITY_TEST_DATABASE_URL`; plain `mise run test` stays unit-only.

## Testing cross-cell behaviour

`internal/multicellular` is the cross-jurisdiction suite — several real cells
(embedded NATS + real Postgres each) driven over real transport; the only CI suite
that's cross-cell, real-transport, and real-store at once. See its README for the DSL.

Add or extend a scenario there when a change affects behaviour that only appears
when ≥2 cells (placements) interact, or depends on an event crossing cells: activity
forwarding (origin / `repo_group` keying, dedup, the `/me` pull gate), settings
fan-out (`settingsrelay` / `settingsconsumer` / `mirrorlifecycle`), placement-
dependent `/me` resolution, or any NATS consumer / cross-cell event / fan-out flag.
Single-cell behaviour stays in the `httpapi` / `store` / `test:pipeline` suites.

New scenarios: wire events only (`cell.Receives` / `cell.API` / `w.Settle`), and
mutation-verify — revert the fix it guards and confirm it fails.

Fair — I got ahead of us: I already committed the "ownership is not reach" decision to the spec (`f24434d70`), and the thread actually leans *multiple* ways on that exact point, including your own earlier position. Happy to revert or hold it; flagging that first. Artifact also on hold until these settle.

The thread's substantive points, as considerations:

**1. Cross-project reach — genuinely unsettled, three positions live in the thread.**
- *Spanning membership* (what I committed): a trail's members can be CRs in any project. James's Jira-spaces argument supports it (reply 47: no spanning → one mega-container or parallel hierarchies).
- *Linked-only* — **your own opening position** (reply 2: "trails would not span projects and have to be 'linked'"): membership stays within the owning project; cross-project intent is parent/related edges between trails. Cleaner permission story (a project-gated trail never references objects outside its gate); cost is two trails + edges for one piece of work.
- *The dissolving observation*: Russell's model (reply 49) + your reply 40 suggest the motivating case (cli in `entireio`, web in `entirehq`) may not be a cross-project case at all natively — one "Entire" project can own both repos regardless of the GitHub-org split, since native structure isn't welded to GitHub's. If that's the intended shape, linked-only loses most of its cost, because same-project covers the common case.

My read: the real question is whether native project structure is *expected* to unify what GitHub splits. If yes → linked-only is defensible and simpler; if project boundaries will mirror forge boundaries in practice → spanning membership earns its keep. That's a product stance, not a schema one.

**2. Org-level.** Your replies 5-6 (org trail with project-trail children, relationship-based not contained) are exactly what the spec has — org scope deferred, relations cover grouping. No tension; the thread just hasn't seen the spec.

**3. Naming.** Contested (Cole anti-GH-terminology, Russell "people will call them PRs anyway", others saying "changes"). Cole explicitly wants this closer to implementation — so the artifact should present "change request" as a working title with the rationale, decision deliberately open.

**4. Non-org users (James).** Real dependency, not just a Q&A: every trail needs a home project, so account-only users need one to exist — account-owned projects are already supported (COR-561), but COR-78 (auto-create personal org/project) is open and this design adds a reason to resolve it.

**5. Definitions gap (Russell/marvin).** "Project" exists only in SpiceDB schema, not prose, and the tenancy boundary is the org. Hardening `Project.Region` into a storage contract makes the missing definition sharper — a glossary/RFD addition is a natural companion piece, arguably a prerequisite for pitching this to the team.

Where do you land on 1? That's the one that changes the spec — and whether I revert `f24434d70` or reshape it.

content.text:
Yes — that's the clean separation. Home answers three things only: **where the trail's row lives** (jurisdiction via the home's region — org rows carry one too), **its number** (`(home, number)`), and **whose permission gate reads it**. Two rules fall out of attachability that are worth stating, because our one-CR-per-trail decision makes attachment stronger than linking:

1. **Attaching a CR is a claim, not a reference.** Exclusive membership means attaching CR X to trail T takes X away from any other trail's possible use. So the write rule has to be dual: attach/detach requires write on the trail (its home's permission) **and** write on the CR's repo. Otherwise anyone with a trail can capture CRs out of repos they can't touch.
2. **Parenting is a claim on the child.** One-parent-max means setting `parent(B) = A` consumes B's parent slot — so it requires write on **B** (the child), plus read on A. Same shape as Linear.

With those two rules, unconstrained reach is safe: a trail can attach CRs from any repo and parent trails from any project the actor can actually write, and the shallow-not-hidden render covers viewers who can't see a member's home.

input.content:
Direction · Trails

Trails, Reshaped

A trail becomes the coordination artifact: one piece of intent that can span several changes, several repos, and several forges. The thing you review and ship today doesn't go away — it becomes the trail's member unit, working title change request.

Summary of the direction for discussion. Details live in the design spec; this page is deliberately the high-level shape.

The model

One trail, many changes

Today one trail is one change — one branch, at most one PR. That's the wrong altitude for intent: real work is a feature across repos, a stack of dependent changes, or an epic with children. The split:

Trail Unified activity feed home: project entire
change requestentire-api #214merged
change requestentire-web #78open
externalgithub.com/foo/bar #91 ↗open
parent Activity platform blocks Feed rollout related Notifications v2

A trail carries the intent (title, body, status rolled up from its members), an ordered set of members — native change requests and external PRs — and typed relations to other trails: parent-child, related, blocks.

What stays, what changes

The change request keeps everything

  • Branch, diff, merge flow — as today
  • Runners, gates, findings, review threads
  • Sessions and checkpoints attach here
  • Its own body, scoped to that change
  • Its existing number — nothing renumbers

The trail moves up a level

  • Lives at project level, not repo level
  • Carries the intent body — with edit history, so you can see how intent evolved
  • Status is a rollup: shipped when every member has shipped
  • Every existing trail gets wrapped 1:1 — no data lost, intent seeded from its change

Key properties

Three ideas carry the design

Home is an address, not a boundary

A trail's home project answers three things: where it's stored (the project's jurisdiction), its number, and who can read it. Home does not limit what the trail may contain — members can come from any repo in any project you can write. And because home carries so little meaning, org-homed trails later are a small additive step, not a redesign.

Attaching is a claim

A change request belongs to exactly one trail, so attaching it is a claim, not a link. Claims need write access on both sides: the trail and the change's repo. Same for parenting a trail — it consumes the child's single parent slot, so it needs write on the child. Cross-project sharing that shouldn't move anything uses related edges instead.

External changes are first-class members

A PR on GitHub (or any forge) can be a trail member alongside native change requests. Where we have an app installation it stays live via webhooks; where we don't, it refreshes opportunistically and says how fresh it is. "Everything shipped" means the external ones merged too.

From the thread

Questions this answers

Non-org users?

Trails need a home project; projects can already be account-owned, so personal users work. Whether we auto-create a personal project per user is COR-78 — this design adds a reason to settle it.

cli is in entireio, web is in entirehq?

Covered twice over. Reach spans projects, so one trail can hold both. And native structure isn't welded to GitHub's: one native project can own repos from several GitHub orgs, which keeps most of this same-project anyway.

Where do runner results and sessions live?

On the change request, exactly as today. The trail only rolls up.

Old PR links?

Links already injected into GitHub PR bodies keep resolving via a redirect. Existing numbers stay with the change they've always identified.

Deliberately unsettled

Open questions

naming What do we call the member unit?

"Change request" is a working title — collision-free (no forge uses it) and Gerrit-adjacent, but the room has floated "changes" and nobody loves GitHub-flavoured vocabulary. Decision deferred until closer to implementation, per Cole.

structure What is a Project, in writing?

The org/project/repo hierarchy exists in code but "Project" has no prose definition. This design leans on projects (home, permissions, jurisdiction), so a short glossary/RFD is a natural companion piece.

defaults Personal org/project auto-creation

COR-78, still open. Not a blocker — account-owned projects exist — but worth resolving alongside.

Delivery

Four slices, each ships alone

01

Rename

Today's trail becomes the change request, everywhere, while it's still internal-only. No behaviour change.

02

Containers

Project-level trails, membership, relations; every existing change wrapped 1:1.

03

Intent history

Edit history on trail and change bodies. Independent — can run in parallel.

04

External changes

Forge PRs as members, live where installed.

Trail direction · 2026-08-24 · full spec in entire-api docs/superpowers/specs

content.text:
Right — and the codebase already asserts this at one level: the unique `(repo_id, gh_pr_id)` constraint exists precisely because "a provider change proposal must never materialize as two trails". A PR on an entire-managed repo always gets a CR twin (trailprensure materializes it), so for managed repos, PR-and-CR are already one thing: the PR is the CR's forge materialization, one member.

The wrinkle bites in the seam between the two member kinds. The underlying entity is the **changeset**, and a member is really a *reference to a changeset* at one of two resolutions — rich (a native CR exists) or thin (forge coordinates only). Two failure modes if we treat them as independent:

1. **Attach-time duplication**: someone attaches `github.com/entirehq/entire-web#78` as an external ref — but that repo is entire-managed, so PR 78 already has a CR twin. Naive design: two member rows, one changeset.
2. **Onboarding duplication**: an external member's repo later joins entire; trailprensure materializes a CR for its PR, and now the trail holds a thin and a rich view of the same changeset.

The fix is an invariant plus two mechanisms, regardless of table layout:

- **Invariant: one changeset appears at most once per trail, at its richest available resolution.** This is the membership-layer extension of the existing `(repo_id, gh_pr_id)` uniqueness.
- **Attach-time resolution**: attaching forge coordinates first checks whether they resolve to an entire-managed repo; if so, the attachment *is* the native CR (materializing it if needed) — the external path is only for genuinely unmanaged repos.
- **Promotion on onboarding**: when a repo joins entire, external members pointing into it get promoted to native CR members (same ordinal, same trail), not duplicated.

This is also a mild argument for revisiting the two-table split — sharing one identity space (forge coordinates) makes promotion an update instead of a cross-table move. I'd still keep the split (a thin ref and a CR have almost no fields in common), but the external table's unique key should be `(forge, remote_repo, remote_number)` *per trail globally*, mirroring CR exclusivity, so promotion is unambiguous.

Want this folded into the spec as an amendment to the external-changes decision (invariant + resolution + promotion), or is there more to the wrinkle you were musing on — e.g. the same changeset appearing in *two different trails* as external-here, native-there?

Correction first: I mis-glossed trailprensure. It repairs the *other* direction — "creates and links missing trail proposals": a trail whose forge PR went missing gets one re-created (trail → PR). The PR-arrives-without-a-trail direction lives in the forge-event/ingest path (`trail_building_state`). The design point survives — a "ensure the rich twin exists" mechanism is what attach-time resolution needs — but I had the arrow backwards on that package.

On the SHA musing — I'd put it this way: **SHAs are the changeset's versions, not its identity.** The set-of-shas mutates at every force-push and rebase, and then once more at merge, where a squash or rebase-merge mints a commit that was never anyone's head (those branches never even become ancestors of main — our own tooling has been bitten by exactly that). So nothing durable can key on SHAs. Two precedents already agree:

- **Gerrit's `Change-Id` trailer** exists precisely because commit SHAs can't identify a change across amends — they had to invent a stable handle above the SHAs.
- **Our own `code_versions` table** already models this correctly: a time-series of `(base_sha, head_sha)` pairs under a stable trail id. The SHA-set is a *history* hanging off the identity, not the identity.

So for the model: the durable handle for a changeset is the CR id for native members and `(forge, repo, number)` for external ones — the same key the dedup/promotion invariant uses. SHAs live one level down, as attributes that version over time and get one final mutation at merge (head → merged-as). Nothing — membership, exclusivity, cross-trail dedup, "did it land" — ever compares SHAs; "did it land" is CR/forge merge *state*, not SHA ancestry.

The "may not be independent" instinct fully lands then: PR and CR are two handles on one identity, unified at attach/onboard time by the resolution+promotion rules, and the SHA-set underneath is shared version history, not a second identity to reconcile.

Fold into the spec as one amendment — changeset identity + the invariant/resolution/promotion trio from before?

I wonder if we want to somehow manage the linkage? because when we read it back later:
Trail 123
changeset 1: PR 242@repo X | CR 78@repo X
changeset 2: CR 924@repo Y
changeset 3: PR243@repo X | CR 79@repo X

content.text:
That read-back is the tell that the changeset wants to be *reified* — a row of its own, not an implicit concept smeared across two tables. And it reverses my earlier two-table position, for a reason worth naming: we keep circling this seam (dedup, promotion, now read-back), and friction that recurring is the design saying the split is wrong. One table, where **the member row is the changeset**:

`trail_changesets`: own `id` (stable), `trail_id`, `ordinal`, and exactly one handle at a time —
- **native**: `(repo_id, change_request_id)`
- **external**: `(forge, remote_repo, remote_number)` + cached state

Then the linkage properties you're asking about fall out:

- **Read-back is exactly your sketch.** `changeset 1: PR 242@repo X | CR 78@repo X` — the CR handle is stored; the PR handle is **derived at read time from the CR's own forge link**, never stored a second time. That's the one rule that keeps linkage manageable: the CR row stays the single writer of "which PR am I" (all the webhook machinery already keys on it), and the trail layer never holds a copy that can disagree. External changesets are the only ones that store forge coordinates directly, because there's no CR to derive from.
- **Promotion is an update, not a row swap.** Repo gets onboarded → the changeset row swaps its external handle for a native one; `id` and `ordinal` stay put, anything hanging off the changeset (comments later, history) survives. The old external coordinates can stay as provenance columns if we want the audit trail of "this entered as a bare PR link".
- **The invariants get structural**: one-changeset-once is row uniqueness (unique on the native ref, unique on the external ref, each across all trails — which also gives cross-trail exclusivity for external members, matching CRs); "richest available resolution" is just which handle group is populated.
- **PR churn is absorbed**: a PR closed and reopened under a new number changes the CR's forge link, and the changeset's read-back follows it automatically — nothing at the trail layer to fix up.

The spec amendment then becomes one coherent change: replace membership + external-changes tables with `trail_changesets`, plus the identity paragraph (handles not SHAs; SHAs are version history with one final mutation at merge) and the attach-time-resolution rule (forge coords that resolve to a managed repo attach as native).

Fold it in like that?

content.text:
That inverts where the polymorphism lives, and I think it's the wrong side of the seam — though the two converge more than they first appear, which may be what makes it tempting.

**CR-as-only-member** means an external PR must be represented *as a CR* — a CR with no branch, no runners, no gates, no repo store to live in (it references a repo entire doesn't manage), and no natural number (CR numbers are per-repo sequences of repos we host). That's a degenerate second kind of CR, and it lands in the heavy domain: every one of the ~38 CR consumers — runner triggers, gate recompute, webhook processing, review machinery — inherits an "is this one real?" branch. That's exactly the silent-failure surface we know this codebase punishes (the class of bugs where one arm of a check quietly never fires). Promotion also gets worse, not better: external→native becomes a cross-store *move* (thin CR in the trail's home store → real CR in the repo's cell) plus a renumbering, instead of an in-place handle swap.

**Changeset-as-member** keeps the CR domain pure — a CR is always repo-backed, always has its full machinery — and puts the two-armed variant in the new, light trail layer where only new code sees it.

The convergence: from the API/UI side, the changeset model *already gives you* the homogeneous first-class member you're describing. A trail's members read back as one uniform list of changesets, each carrying an optional CR handle and a forge handle (derived from the CR when native, stored when external). Nobody consuming a trail ever sees two member types. The difference is only underneath: whether the thin case is a degenerate CR contaminating the heavy domain, or a handle-arm on the changeset row in the light one.

So my recommendation stands: **changeset reified at the trail layer, CR stays strictly repo-backed**. If the deciding instinct is "members should feel first-class and uniform" — that's satisfied; the changeset *is* the first-class object.

Settle on that and I'll fold the whole amendment in (changeset table replacing membership + external-changes, identity-not-SHAs, attach-time resolution, promotion-in-place)?

content.text:
That's the strongest move yet — it deletes the second path instead of teaching both paths to coexist. If every member must be a CR on our side, then the way to track work in a repo we don't manage is the platform's own answer: **bring the repo in as a mirror, and its PR materializes a real CR through the normal forge-event path**. The entire external-member apparatus dissolves:

- No two-armed changeset, no `trail_external_changes`, no promotion machinery, no attach-time resolution polymorphism — membership goes back to the simple table: `(trail_id, repo_id, change_request_id, ordinal)`, exactly as first specced.
- The changeset-identity discussion still pays off, but it collapses to one sentence: the CR *is* the changeset's durable identity; SHAs underneath are version history with one final mutation at merge; the PR handle is derived from the CR's forge link. Your read-back (`PR 242@repo X | CR 78@repo X`) works unchanged — one row, two displayed handles.
- Slice 4 as designed mostly evaporates.

Two things to accept explicitly with it:

1. **A scope cut**: a stateful reference to a PR in a repo we *can't* mirror (someone else's private repo, a forge with no integration) is no longer possible. The fallback is plain informational **links** on a trail — a URL, no state, not a member, ignored by rollup. Given external tracking was never one of your drivers, I think this trade is right, and links can be upgraded later if it ever becomes one.
2. **A sync caveat to verify at implementation time**: PRs materialize CRs via webhook deliveries, which need an app installation on the mirrored repo. For third-party mirrors without one, CRs on that mirror may need the opportunistic-poll tier — smaller than the old slice 4, but not zero. (And per the repo's standing rule: any new service-forge reason gets registered in Core in the same change, or it ships dead.)

If both are acceptable, the amendment I fold in becomes: members are native CRs only; mirror-first for external work; trail links for the untrackable; changeset identity = CR, SHAs are versions; slice 4 replaced by "trail links + mirror-gap poll tier". Confirm and I'll update the spec and the artifact together.

attachment.snippet:
1	# Trails as containers of change requests
2	
3	Status: approved design, pre-implementation.
4	Scope: entire-api (primary), entiredb Core (one companion change), entire.io + CLI (rename-window coordination).
5	
6	## Summary
7	
8	Today 1 trail = 1 change: a `repo_trails` row carries the branch, head/base SHAs,
9	at most one forge PR, a body, and all runner/gate/finding machinery. This design
10	splits that into two objects:
11	
12	- **Change request (CR)** — today's row, renamed. The unit of shipping: branch,
13	  SHAs, forge link, its own body scoped to that change, runners, gates,
14	  findings, threads. Always lives in its repo's cell store. Keeps the existing
15	  per-repo `number` sequence and every existing value.
16	- **Trail (container)** — a new project-level object that owns intent: title,
17	  intent body (editor document), status rollup, an ordered set of member CRs, and typed relations to other trails (parent / related /
18	  blocks). Numbered per-project, stored in the project's home jurisdiction.
19	
20	Naming rule (write once, in the change-request package doc): **proposal** = the
21	forge-side artifact (trailforge vocabulary: `ChangeProposalRef`,
22	`EnsureTrailChangeProposal`, …); **request** = the entire domain object that may
23	materialize as one. A change request exists before any forge object does;
24	`changeRequest.Proposal` is the boundary reading. No forge uses "change
25	request" as a native term, so it is collision-free; Gerrit's "Change" is the
26	closest precedent for the semantics.
27	
28	Drivers (in priority order): multi-repo features, stacked/sequenced changes,
29	epic-style organisation. External work is tracked mirror-first (decision 9),
30	not via a member kind.
31	
32	## Decisions
33	
34	Each of these was made explicitly during design; the rationale lines are the
35	short version.
36	
37	1. **Trail becomes the container; existing trails become CRs.** Migration
38	   backfills a 1:1 wrapper trail per existing CR. The container keeps the
39	   user-facing name "trail" because it is the object that carries intent.
40	2. **Hard rename now, no legacy names left behind.** Trails are internal-only
41	   today; there will never be a cheaper moment. The physical table, Go types,
42	   HTTP routes, and backlink template all rename in one slice.
43	3. **CRs keep the existing numbers.** The current per-repo trail number
44	   identifies the change (it is 1:1 with the PR and baked into forge
45	   backlinks), so it travels with the CR row. The `number` column does not
46	   move. Trails get a fresh per-project sequence.
47	4. **Trails are project-level only.** No repo-scoped or org-scoped trails.
48	   Involved repos are derived from membership (each membership row carries
49	   `repo_id`). Org-level grouping is expressible with cross-project relations;
50	   a true org scope would be additive later. This kills scope polymorphism,
51	   the promotion dance, and repo-trail/CR number ambiguity.
52	5. **Trail home = the project's jurisdiction.** Core's `projects.region`
53	   already exists on every project row; today it is a non-enforced hint
54	   (`core/resource/store.go:1488` — race-minted for mirrors projects). It gets
55	   hardened into a contract for trail storage: a project's trails live in the
56	   cell serving that jurisdiction (jurisdiction→cell is 1:1 in current
57	   topology). Mirrors projects either never hold trails or get their region
58	   fixed first. Repo-level machinery (CRs, runners, gates, webhooks) stays in
59	   the repo's cell untouched.
60	6. **Home is an address; attachability is the policy.** A trail's home (its
61	   owning project) answers exactly three things: where the row is stored
62	   (jurisdiction via the home's region), its number (`(home, number)`), and
63	   whose permission gate reads it. Home is not a semantic boundary on what
64	   the trail may contain. Because home carries so little meaning, org-homed
65	   trails are a cheap later addition (`home_type` + `home_id` instead of a
66	   bare `project_id`), not a different feature — v1 homes are projects only.
67	
68	   Reach is instead governed by two write rules, both consequences of
69	   attachment being exclusive (decision 7), which makes attaching a claim
70	   rather than a reference:

message.content: Q: would this design support runners at the trail level in future?

content.text:
Yes — additively, and a few decisions already made are quietly load-bearing for it:

**What's already in place as seams:**
- **A trigger surface exists.** The stored-rollup decision means there's already a "trail state changed" code path — the recompute hook fires on member CR state change and membership change, and body edits produce revision events. Trail-level runners are consumers of exactly those hooks; no new eventing concept needed.
- **A place to run and store.** The trail lives in one deterministic cell (the project's jurisdiction), so trail-scoped runner/gate result tables land in the home store using the same trail-scoped patterns the CR side already uses. The container being machinery-light was the point: adding machinery to it later is tables-plus-triggers, not a rework.
- **A stable input for intent-aware runners.** Body revisions give a trail runner something CR runners never had: it can pin "evaluated intent at revision N" and re-run when intent changes — the audit-history slice accidentally builds the input contract for an intent-vs-implementation runner.
- **CR-level machinery is untouched underneath**, so trail runners compose over CR results (e.g. "all member gates green + trail-level review passed") rather than replacing anything.

**The two real gaps a future slice would have to close:**
1. **Cross-cell deep reads.** v1 renders cross-cell members shallow. A trail runner that needs member *diffs* from another cell needs the deep resolution we explicitly deferred — same-cell trails work day one, cross-cell trail runners wait on that.
2. **Config and credentials.** Runner config is per-repo today; trail runners need project-level config (natural home exists — the project) and per-repo forge tokens for each member repo they read, which means the service-forge reason registration constraint applies once per capability, and a runner spanning N repos does N mints.

One thing to keep deliberate when it comes: trail-level *gates that block CR merges* would couple a repo-cell merge path to home-cell trail state — a cross-cell read on the hot path. Trail gates should gate the *trail* (its own shippable status), not reach down to block member merges, at least until someone has a concrete need worth that coupling.

Worth a one-line "future: trail-level runners" note in the spec's design so the seams don't get accidentally closed? It's the kind of thing slice 2's implementer could otherwise flatten (e.g. by inlining the rollup recompute instead of keeping it a hook).

Technically yes, and this chain even qualifies under the house rule (stack only when it genuinely won't build — 2b won't compile without slice 1's renamed types, 2c needs 2b's store layer). But I'd hold the default and stack *reactively*, not upfront:

**Why not a standing stack here:**
- Every review wave on a base PR costs a rebase per PR above it, and our loop (bugbot + trail findings + steward waves) reliably produces waves. We've been burned on exactly this — a PR still drawing findings isn't a base.
- Stack tooling (Graphite, ghstack, gh-stack — GitHub has no native stacks) wants to push to GitHub and drive its PR API directly. Our origin is `entire://` and mirrors through; direct-to-GitHub pushes are the thing we've specifically stopped doing. The tools fight the mirror model.

**What the shape of this work actually favours — fast sequence over stack:** slice 1 is mechanical with "existing suites pass" as its whole verification, so it should merge in a day or two, and 2b starts on main right after. Meanwhile 2a and slice 3 run genuinely parallel with no base at all. A stack buys you overlap on the 1→2b seam only, and that seam is short.

**When to stack anyway, and how:** if slice 1 (or 2b) stalls in review while its dependent is done, stack just that pair, manually — branch 2b off the slice-1 branch, `gh pr create -B <slice-1-branch>`, name the merge order in the PR body. GitHub auto-retargets the base to main when the parent merges and its branch is deleted. No tooling, mirror-safe, and it's the one-PR-deep stack the rules allow rather than a standing tower.

So: plan for sequential-fast with 2a/3 parallel; stack tactically only if review latency actually materializes on the critical path. Go on that basis?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/alex/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.3.0/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

### 1. Project.Region: where set/read

**Struct definition** — `core/model/types.go:251-258`
```go

	OwnerType string // "account", "org"
	OwnerID   ID     // polymorphic: AccountID or OrgID

	CreatedAt time.Time
}
```

**Migrations** (projects table, `core/resource/migrations/`):
- `001_tables.sql:37-44` — creates `projects` with `region TEXT NOT NULL` (no FK, no CHECK constraint, no enum).
- No later migration in `core/resource/migrations/` adds a check constraint or enum on `projects.region` (searched, none found).

**Writes**:
- `core/resource/store.go:1407` `CreateProject(ctx, name, ownerType, ownerID, region string)` — sets `p.Region = region` at line 1421. No validation of `region` value.
- `core/resource/store.go:1514` `CreateOrFindMirrorsProject(ctx, ownerType, ownerID, jurisdiction string)` — sets `p.Region = jurisdiction` at line 1540. Doc comment lines 1488-1494 is the load-bearing caveat:
  > "jurisdiction seeds Project.Region on first create only — a non-enforced hint (Project.Region carries no per-cluster meaning once one project spans every cluster an owner mirrors into) that simply reflects whichever cluster's mirror-create won the race to mint the project."
- `core/coreapi/projects.go:33` `CreateProject` handler — line 44-47: `region := in.Body.Region; if region == "" { region = s.Server.Jurisdiction() }`. Client-supplied region string is passed through **verbatim, with no allowlist/enum check**.

**A. Public/authenticated corev1 HTTP API** (huma-based, end-user or service-account bearer auth via `api.ClaimsFromContext`):
- `api/corev1/projects.go:6-13` — `Project` wire type **already includes `Region string `json:"region"``.

- `core/coreapi/repos.go:3364` `LookupBySlug` (`et/{project}/{repo}` and `gh/{owner}/{repo}`) — **unauthenticated**, returns `{repoId, cell, jurisdiction, owner, repo}` (`corev1.LookupBySlugOutput`), but only for repos with the `public_viewer` grant (core/coreapi/repos.go:3384-3408). Not usable for private-project lookups.

**B. Internal mTLS Connect-RPC surface** (`proto/internalapi/*`, workload-gated, no end-user identity) — this is the actual service-facing pattern:
- `proto/internalapi/repodirectory/v1/repodirectory.proto:1-8,32-50` — `RepoDirectory.BatchGet(repo_ids) -> ResolvedRepo{repo_id, repo_name, project_id, project_name, owner_type/id/name, url, jurisdiction, cluster_slug, mirror}`. **This is the "resolver_test.go showed Jurisdiction+ClusterSlug per repo" surface** — confirmed at `core/repodirectory/resolver.go:52-61` (`RepoCore{Jurisdiction, ClusterSlug}`) and `resolver_test.go:44-58`.
  - Gated to `servicetoken.WorkloadPeregrine, servicetoken.WorkloadEntireSearch` — **`internal/entirecore/internal_listener.go:571-573`. entire-api is NOT in this allowlist today.**
- `proto/internalapi/repofacts/v1/repofacts.proto` + `core/repofacts/handler.go` — push-only (entire-api → Core), gated to `servicetoken.WorkloadEntireAPI` (`internal/entirecore/internal_listener.go:581-583`).
- `proto/internalapi/repolookup/v1/repolookup.proto:1-8` — mirror/native-mirror routing lookups, gated to `WorkloadWebhookIngest, WorkloadMirrorWorker, WorkloadFanout, WorkloadMetaFanout, WorkloadCoreFanout, …` (`internal_listener.go:590-598`) — entire-api not in this allowlist either.

**No existing endpoint returns project→jurisdiction as a service-facing (mTLS, workload-gated) call.** The public `GetProject` returns region but requires user/claims auth; `RepoDirectory.BatchGet` returns per-repo jurisdiction+project_id but is gated to Peregrine/EntireSearch, not entire-api, and is repo-keyed, not project-keyed. **There is no `ProjectDirectory`-equivalent internal RPC today.**

### 3. Jurisdiction / cluster_slug meaning

- `core/resource/migrations/003_repo_registry.sql:1-12` — renamed the old global `repos` table to `repo_registry` and its `region` column to `jurisdiction`.
- `core/resource/migrations/012_repo_registry_cluster_slug.sql:1-21` — adds `repo_registry.cluster_slug TEXT` (nullable, slug not opaque ID: "slug is the load-bearing identifier in JWT auds (`service:entiredb:<slug>`)").
- Jurisdiction→cluster resolution: `core/api/accessors.go:409-418` `Server.ClusterCellAndJurisdiction(ctx, slug) (cell, jurisdiction string, err error)` looks up `s.cluster.GetBySlugGlobal(ctx, slug)` and returns `c.Cell, c.Jurisdiction`.
- The authoritative source of jurisdiction values is the **clusters registry/fixture**, not project rows: `core/cluster/fixture.go:41` (`Jurisdiction string` yaml field, required at line 138) and `core/cluster/fixtures/clusters.staging.yaml:19,56,75,93` — jurisdiction values observed: `us`, `eu` (comment also mentions `local`).
- **Is there a projects equivalent of repo_registry? No.** `projects` has one flat `region TEXT NOT NULL` column (`001_tables.sql:37-44`), no `cluster_slug`, no per-placement rows, and (per the doc comment at store.go:1488-1494) is explicitly documented as carrying no enforced per-cluster meaning. `repo_registry` by contrast tracks `jurisdiction` + `cluster_slug` per repo row, resolved through the clusters table.

Copy the shape of **`core/repodirectory`** (batch read) or **`core/repofacts`** (single-workload push) — both are Connect-RPC internal APIs:

1. Proto in `proto/internalapi/<name>/v1/<name>.proto` (see `proto/internalapi/repodirectory/v1/repodirectory.proto`), generated via `mise-tasks/protobuf` into `gen/proto/internalapi/<name>/v1/`.
2. Handler package `core/<name>/connect.go` implementing the generated Connect interface (`core/repodirectory/connect.go:12-19`, `core/repofacts/handler.go:29-34`) — interfaces for its store deps so fakes work in tests (`resolver.go:63-74`, `handler.go:24-27`).
3. Mount + gate in `internal/entirecore/internal_listener.go`:
   - Build handler + Connect mux entry (pattern at lines 297-300 for repodirectory, 307-310 for repofacts).
   - Add a `<name>AuthMiddleware(trustDomain string) func(http.Handler) http.Handler` returning `svctokserver.WorkloadGate(trustDomain, <allowed workloads>...)` (lines 571-573, 581-583, 590-598) — auth model for service callers is **mTLS + per-listener workload allowlist**, no SpiceDB, no end-user identity (`repodirectory.proto:6-8`, `repofacts.proto` comment `core/repofacts/handler.go:3-4`).
4. For a project→jurisdiction lookup specifically for entire-api, `servicetoken.WorkloadEntireAPI` (`core/servicetoken/workload.go:29`) is the const to add to the new gate's allowlist — the same const already used at `internal_listener.go:582` for RepoFacts.

**Best exemplar to copy**: `core/repodirectory/` (proto, resolver.go, connect.go) — it's read-only, batch-keyed, already resolves `jurisdiction`/`cluster_slug` off `model.Project`/cluster lookups, and its test (`resolver_test.go`) shows the fake-based test convention.

### 5. Existing validation/enforcement on region values

**None found.** `CreateProject` (`core/coreapi/projects.go:44-47`) takes `in.Body.Region` verbatim or defaults to `s.Server.Jurisdiction()` — no enum, no check against the clusters/topology registry. `api/corev1/projects.go:21` (`CreateProjectInput.Body.Region`) has no `enum:` struct tag (contrast with `OwnerType string `enum:"org,account"`` at line 19/9). ### 6. Test conventions / exemplar

- corev1/coreapi handler tests live in `core/coreapi/*_test.go`, package `coreapi` (not `_test`), using in-package helpers like `setupReposServerJur(t, nil, "us")`, `reposClaims(owner)`, `shortUniq(...)`, `seedProject(t, res)`, `seedCluster(t, pool, slug, jurisdiction, cell)`. - `mise run test` (`mise-tasks/test/_default`) — short tests; flags `--race`, `--verbose`, `--shard {all|db|nodb}`, `--run <regex>`, `--count <n>`. syntax = "proto3";

```proto
package internalapi.projectdirectory.v1;

// ProjectDirectory resolves project metadata for trusted internal services.
// Served on the internal mTLS listener; callers are gated by workload
// identity (no end-user identity is involved). Read-only.
service ProjectDirectory {
  rpc BatchGet(BatchGetRequest) returns (BatchGetResponse);
}

message BatchGetRequest {
  repeated string project_ids = 1;
}

}

message BatchGetResponse {

  repeated ResolvedProject projects = 1;
}
```

### Migration tooling/conventions
- Goose-managed, one set per store under `internal/store/migrations/{repo,user}/`, embedded + applied out-of-band via `migrate` subcommand (CONTRIBUTING.md:13-18).
- **Mandatory naming**: new files must be `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_<name>.sql` (UTC timestamp) — never a hand-picked integer (CONTRIBUTING.md:22-33). Old `001…050` integer files are grandfathered and left alone.
- Scaffold: `scripts/new-migration.sh <repo|user> <name>` → writes `internal/store/migrations/$store/${ts}_${name}.sql` with `SET search_path TO repo|usr, public;` stubs (scripts/new-migration.sh:28-46).
- Any trail→change migration must follow this convention (timestamped filename via `scripts/new-migration.sh repo <name>`), never renumber the legacy `0NN` files.

The entire-api inventory is in, and it surfaced something the spec's "one honest sweep" didn't account for — the rename has a third category beyond code and routes: **wire-visible and persisted identifiers**, where a blind rename breaks running systems. This needs your call before I finish the slice-1 plan. The principled line I propose:

**Rename (domain vocabulary — the container will collide with it):**
- Everything already planned: table + 20 child tables/indexes, ~800 Go identifiers, routes, operation IDs, OpenAPI tags, JSON response fields (`trailId`→`changeId` etc. — breaking, but inside the coordinated BFF/CLI window), the backlink URL segment.
- **Persisted values the container will genuinely collide with**: `editor_documents.entity_type='trail'` rows (the container will also have body docs — old rows *must* become `'change'` or the two objects share an identity space), `trail_legacy_id_map.entity_type`, the `repo_setting_kv` key `'trails'` (backfill migration, same pattern as the existing gates backfill), and runner-config `"scope":"trail"` in stored JSONB **plus a permanent dual-read alias** in the decoder, because repo owners' `.entire/` config files say `scope: trail` and we can't rewrite their repos.

**Keep as legacy spellings (opaque infra identifiers, documented once):**
- NATS stream/subject names (`trail_events_v1`, `trail_forge.v1.*`) — provisioned declaratively in fleet, and the contract doc says wire tokens are "never rename once shipped". The events they carry are *about* changes; if the container needs events later it gets a new stream. Renaming these is a coordinated fleet change purchased for zero behaviour.
- Event type tokens (`trail.created`…) and payload fields — same contract.
- PR-body sentinels (`<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->`) — already embedded in live GitHub PR bodies forever; renaming means dual-recognition logic for no user-visible gain. Keep, write the same markers.

**Needs a look before deciding:** `authz.TrailType = "trail"` (SpiceDB resource type). If it's schema + per-trail tuples, renaming is a real authz data migration and the container needs its own resource name anyway; if it's local vocab only, it folds into the Go rename. I'll have the planner check `internal/authz/local.go` and the SpiceDB schema before committing either way.

This keeps "no legacy names left behind" where names are *vocabulary* (what people read and the container collides with), and tolerates legacy spelling only where the name is an opaque routing key with external coordination cost. Sign off on that line — or push it harder/softer — and I'll finish the slice-1 plan accordingly. (Slice 2a's plan is already written; the entire.io/CLI inventory is still running.)

# Slice 1: Trail → Change Rename Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Rename the existing trail domain object to "change" across every repo and wire surface, freeing the name "trail" for the container object (slice 2), leaving no legacy names except the documented exceptions.

**Architecture:** Five repos in dependency order: fleet (new NATS streams) and entiredb (SpiceDB `change` type) first — both additive and deploy-safe alone; then entire-api in two PRs (1a: everything externally invisible — table+data migrations, Go rename, NATS cutover; 1b: API surface rename with old routes kept as deprecated twins); then entire.io and cli against the new surface; then a small entire-api follow-up removing the deprecated twins and the NATS drain.

**Tech Stack:** Go (entire-api, cli), goose migrations, NATS JetStream (fleet-provisioned), SpiceDB (entiredb-owned schema), TypeScript/Hono/TanStack (entire.io), mise everywhere.

**Spec:** entire-api `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-24-trail-containers-design.md` — sections "Renames (slice 1)" and "Wire contracts and persisted values".

## Global Constraints

- Every repo: work in a worktree (`~/.claude/hooks/worktrees.sh new <branch>`), never on main.
- entire-api gates: `mise run build && mise run vet && mise run lint && mise run test`; plus `mise run test:integration` (Docker) and `mise run test:multicellular` for the migration-touching PR.
- entire-api migrations: `scripts/new-migration.sh repo <name>` only (UTC-timestamp versions); never edit merged migrations; never renumber `0NN` files.
- entire.io gates: root `pnpm format:check` (oxfmt — not covered by lint), `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`.
- cli gates: `mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test`.
- entiredb gates: `mise run lint && mise run test`.
- **Never rename**: NATS stream `trail_events_v1` / `trail_forge_events_v1` internals (they retire, never mutate); PR-body sentinels `<!-- entire-shadow-pr -->`, `<!-- entire-trail-link-start/-end -->` (live in existing GitHub PR bodies — keep byte-identical).
- **Permanent dual-read**: `runnerconfig` decode accepts `"scope":"trail"` and `"trails_review"` as aliases of the new spellings forever (repo owners' `.entire/` files use them).
- PR sizing: PRs 1a and 1b exceed the 800-line hard ceiling; each PR body states the atomic-rename justification explicitly.
- Cross-repo commits made from a session that started elsewhere: run `entire:session-crosslink` after committing, before pushing.

---

### Task 1 (fleet): provision change_events_v1 + change_forge_events_v1

**Files:**
- Modify: the NATS stream manifests under fleet's `apps/nats-streams` (locate with `rg -ln "trail_events_v1" <fleet-repo>` — the nack Stream CRs referenced by entire-api's `internal/trailevents/contract.go:41` comment "provisioned declaratively in fleet").

**Interfaces:**
- Produces: JetStream streams `change_events_v1` (subjects `change_events_v1.>`) and `change_forge_events_v1` (subjects `change_forge.v1.>`), config copied field-for-field from the trail streams they succeed.
- Consumes: nothing; additive.

- [ ] **Step 1:** In the fleet repo, copy each existing trail stream CR to a new file with the new name/subjects; change nothing else (retention, replicas, limits identical). Keep the old CRs — they retire in Task 8.
- [ ] **Step 2:** Validate: whatever fleet's manifest check is (`rg -ln "kustomize|flux" Makefile mise.toml` at fleet root for the build task) — run it.
- [ ] **Step 3:** Commit `feat(nats-streams): change_events_v1 + change_forge_events_v1 (trail streams' successors)`, push, PR, note in body: additive; old streams retire after entire-api cutover completes.
- [ ] **Step 4:** Confirm streams exist in staging after merge (`nats_stream_inspect` via the staging MCP, or fleet's normal rollout check) before starting Task 3.

### Task 2 (entiredb): SpiceDB `change` resource type + tuple migration

**Files:**
- Investigate first (concrete steps below), then: the SpiceDB schema file (locate: `rg -ln "definition trail" <entiredb>` or `rg -ln "trail" core/authz/`), the tuple-writing site(s), and a migration/backfill for existing tuples.

**Interfaces:**
- Produces: SpiceDB definition `change` identical to `trail` (same relations/permissions incl. `write_body`); all existing `trail:*` tuples duplicated to `change:*`; writers write both during the window.
- Consumed by: Task 3's entire-api vocab re-sync (checks against `change`).

- [ ] **Step 1 (investigate, bounded):** In entiredb: `rg -n "\"trail\"|definition trail|TrailType" --type go -g '!gen/**'` and read `core/authz/vocab.go` + the `.zed`/schema source. Identify: (a) schema definition for `trail`, (b) every site writing `trail:*` tuples (likely a batched SpiceDB write near trail/authz registration — `rg -n "WriteRelationships|TouchRelationships" core/ | rg -i trail`), (c) tuple count in staging.
- [ ] **Step 2:** Write failing test: authz check `write_body` on `change:<id>` passes for a subject granted via the same path that grants it on `trail:<id>` (copy the existing trail authz test — find via `rg -ln "TrailType|trail:" core/ --type go -g '*_test.go'`).
- [ ] **Step 3:** Add `change` definition to the schema (copy of `trail`), add dual-write at every writer site (write `trail:*` and `change:*` tuples in the same batch), backfill existing tuples (one-off task/command following whatever backfill pattern entiredb uses — find one: `rg -ln "backfill" core/ --type go` and copy its shape).
- [ ] **Step 4:** Run the test suite; commit `feat(authz): change resource type (trail's successor), dual-write + backfill`; PR. Note in body: `trail` definition + dual-write removed in a follow-up after entire-api's re-synced vocab ships.
- [ ] **Step 5:** After merge + backfill run in staging: verify a known trail's tuples exist under `change:*` before Task 3's PR merges.

### Task 3 (entire-api, PR 1a): internal rename — table, data, Go, NATS cutover

Everything in this PR is externally invisible: no route, no JSON field, no OpenAPI change. Existing HTTP tests must pass unchanged except for identifier renames inside them.

**Files:**
- Create: one migration via `scripts/new-migration.sh repo rename_trails_to_changes` (table + child columns + indexes + persisted values — full list below).
- Modify: all of `internal/store`, and the 54 consumer files across `internal/httpapi`, `internal/trailforgeevents`, `internal/findingsgate`, `internal/gatecheckpublish`, `internal/gaterecompute`, `internal/runnertriggers`, `internal/trailprensure`, `internal/ingest`, `internal/importer`, `internal/planetscale`, `internal/multicellular`, `cmd/import-planetscale`; package directories `internal/trail*` → `internal/change*` equivalents; `internal/trailevents` + `internal/trailforgeevents` stream cutover; `internal/authz` vocab re-sync; `internal/runnerconfig` dual-read.

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: Task 1's streams (must exist in staging before merge), Task 2's `change` SpiceDB type (backfilled).
- Produces: `store.ChangeListRow`, `store.ChangeDetailRow`, table `repo_changes`, packages `internal/changeevents`, `internal/changeforge`, `internal/changeforgeevents`, `internal/changeprensure`, etc. — the names PR 1b and slice 2 build on.

- [ ] **Step 1 — migration:** One SQL migration renaming, in dependency order:
  - `ALTER TABLE repo_trails RENAME TO repo_changes;` and rename its indexes (`repo_trails_repo_number_uq`→`repo_changes_repo_number_uq`, `_repo_branch_uq`, `_repo_status_idx`, `_repo_updated_idx`, `_repo_released_original_branch_idx`, `_repo_gh_pr_id_uq`, `_author_updated_idx` — `ALTER INDEX ... RENAME TO ...`).
  - Child tables rename table AND `trail_id`→`change_id` columns: `repo_trail_numbering`→`repo_change_numbering`, `trail_thread_events`→`change_thread_events` (+sequence), `trail_threads`→`change_threads`, `trail_thread_messages`→`change_thread_messages`, `sandbox_runs.trail_id`→`change_id`, `repo_trail_monitor_results`→`repo_change_monitor_results`, `trail_attachments`→`change_attachments`, `repo_trail_gate_results`→`repo_change_gate_results`, `repo_trail_merge_reservations`→`repo_change_merge_reservations`, `code_versions.trail_id`→`change_id`, `reviews.trail_id`, `review_comments.trail_id`, `code_review_events`/`_sequence` trail_id columns, `trails_outbox`→`changes_outbox`, `trail_legacy_id_map`→`change_legacy_id_map`, `trail_import_state`→`change_import_state`, `repo_trail_branch_forge_state`→`repo_change_branch_forge_state`, `repo_trail_forge_deliveries`→`repo_change_forge_deliveries`, `trail_watch_presence`→`change_watch_presence` — renaming each table's indexes with it (exact names in the inventory; verify each with `\d` against a migrated local DB).
  - Persisted values: `UPDATE editor_documents SET entity_type='change' WHERE entity_type='trail';` `UPDATE change_legacy_id_map SET entity_type='change' WHERE entity_type='trail';` `UPDATE repo_setting_kv SET setting_key='changes' WHERE setting_key='trails';`
  - Stored runner/gate config JSONB (`repo_gate_definitions.config`, `sandbox_runs.output_config`): leave stored rows as-is — the dual-read alias (Step 4) covers them; rewriting opaque JSONB in a migration risks more than it buys. State this in a migration comment.
- [ ] **Step 2 — verify migration:** `mise run test:integration` (store suite runs migrations); then the migration-specific tests that assert on old table names get renamed as part of Step 3.
- [ ] **Step 3 — mechanical Go rename:** scripted, then hand-audited: `Trail`→`Change` / `trail`→`change` across identifiers, SQL strings, file names, package directories (`internal/trailevents`→`internal/changeevents`, `trailforge`→`changeforge`, `trailforgeevents`→`changeforgeevents`, `trailprensure`→`changeprensure`, `trailprlink`→`changeprlink`, `trailsrelay`→`changesrelay`, `trailbuildingstate`→`changebuildingstate`, `trailblobs`→`changeblobs`). # Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" [shape=diamond];
        "Finding conflicts with plan text?" [shape=diamond];
        "Rule on the conflict, ledger the ruling" [shape=box];
        "Fix round R of 5: R≤3 resume implementer; R≥4 fresh implementer, more capable model" [shape=box];
        "Dispatch scoped re-review (./re-review-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "All findings addressed?" [shape=diamond];
        "R = 5?" [shape=diamond];
        "Adjudicate each open finding" [shape=box];
        "Any load-bearing finding?" [shape=diamond];
        "Rule and continue; stop only if every path forward is a guess" [shape=box];
        "Park findings in ledger with rulings" [shape=box];
        "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [shape=box];
    }

    "Setup: worktree, ledger check, read plan, pre-flight review" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer (../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)" [shape=box];
    "Final findings? ONE fix dispatch, one scoped re-review, adjudicate residuals" [shape=box];
    "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Setup: worktree, ledger check, read plan, pre-flight review" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer asks questions?";

    "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Spec ✅ and quality approved?";
    "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [label="yes"];
    "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Finding conflicts with plan text?" [label="no"];
    "Finding conflicts with plan text?" -> "Rule on the conflict, ledger the ruling" [label="yes"];
    "Rule on the conflict, ledger the ruling" -> "Fix round R of 5: R≤3 resume implementer; R≥4 fresh implementer, more capable model";
    "Finding conflicts with plan text?" -> "Fix round R of 5: R≤3 resume implementer; R≥4 fresh implementer, more capable model" [label="no"];
    "Fix round R of 5: R≤3 resume implementer; R≥4 fresh implementer, more capable model" -> "Dispatch scoped re-review (./re-review-prompt.md)";
```
